newsitem.title: USA: U.S. reinsurers' premium growth seen disappointing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. reinsurers' premium growth seen disappointing.

text.p: Reinsurers are likely to report disappointing premium growth even though first quarter earnings should be in line with expectations, analysts said Friday.
They said that premium growth is slowing because prices are soft, and so instead of writing new business at low prices, reinsurers are opting not to write much new business.

"While earnings are likely to come in in line with expectations in general, I think investors are likely to be somewhat disappointed by the growth opportunities for these companies," said Peter Wade, analyst at Lehman Brothers.
Wade said he expects to see continued slowing of top line premium growth, and that that may hurt these stocks.
Although earnings should be relatively stable, premium growth may fall short and "consequently they disappoint," he said.

The reinsurers in Bermuda are likely to be hit the hardest because those companies have much greater exposure to the catastrophe reinsurance market, where the price declines have been the most severe, Wade said.
Bermuda emerged as a major center for reinsurers, which in effect provide insurance to insurance companies, in the early 1990s.
Among the reinsurers based there is PartnerRE Ltd, which is expected to post a slight earnings decline of 0.9 percent to $1.09 per share, according to the First Call consensus of analysts' estimates.

"Regarding the Bermuda companies, it's very evident that prices continue to decline for property-catastrophe reinsurance, both in the U.S. and probably to an even greater extent outside the U.S.," said Jay Cohen, an analyst at Merrill-Lynch.
He said that companies that want to protect underwriting margins and maintain healthy return on equity will see premiums decrease in the first quarter.
Cohen noted that the level of claims in the first quarter would be "very limited" because of the general absence of natural catastrophes.
Reinsurers have generally not seen any major losses since Hurricane Andrew in 1992, said Ira Zuckerman, vice president of research at Nutmeg Securities.
"The cat(astrophe) reinsurance market probably is going to do very well in terms of underwriting results, but the pricing is horrendous," Zuckerman said.

"The better companies, like (Connecticut-based) General Re Corp, are pricing for what the loss requires. But a lot of the reinsurers... are having problems because the pricing is inadequate on commercial lines as well, so that's just getting passed on."
"It's a question of the rich getting richer, and the poor having more problems," Zuckerman said.
He said General Re was an example of a company willing to sacrifice new business in order to maintain pricing and underwriting results.
